title: Trump Jokes About Running for a 'Fourth Term' at White House Dinner
excerpt: President Donald Trump donned a 'Trump 2028' hat and told journalists he intended to run again, before clarifying he was joking. The Constitution bars a third term.
body:
• Trump announced his "intention to run for a fourth term" at the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner on July 24, before saying he was joking
  • He pulled out a red "Trump 2028" hat during the speech, a move that went viral and was reposted by the White House with a laughing emoji
  • The 22nd Amendment explicitly bars any person from being elected president more than twice
  • Trump has repeatedly floated third-term scenarios since 2025, though he also acknowledged the constitutional barrier last October
  • House Speaker Mike Johnson has said he sees no path to amending the Constitution to allow a third term

A 'Scoop' at the Correspondents' Dinner

President Donald Trump used the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Association Dinner on July 24 to deliver what he called "somewhat of a scoop" — announcing his "intention to run for a fourth term as president of the United States," according to USA Today.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=NC37xSB0tX4

"I won three times, now I'm going to do it again," Trump said as he placed a red "Trump 2028" hat on his head, drawing a mix of laughter and groans from the press corps. Trump has won two presidential elections but insists the 2020 race was rigged against him, a claim rejected by courts, audits, and election officials.

Trump then clarified he was "only kidding," and the White House reposted the moment on social media with a laughing face emoji, according to USA Today.

A Pattern of Third-Term Teasing

The dinner bit was the latest in a long string of comments Trump has made about seeking a third term throughout his second presidency. The pattern has included moments of apparent seriousness followed by walk-backs:

In March 2025, Trump told NBC News that "there are methods" by which he could serve a third term, including a scenario where Vice President JD Vance would run in 2028 with Trump as his running mate, then step aside. "I'm not joking," he said at the time, according to Bloomberg.

By August 2025, his tone shifted. Asked on CNBC's Squawk Box if he would run again, Trump said: "No. Probably not... Probably not, I'd like to," according to the Akron Beacon Journal.

"If you read it, it's pretty clear — I'm not allowed to run. It's too bad, but we have a lot of great people."

— Donald Trump, October 2025, aboard Air Force One

The Constitutional Barrier

The 22nd Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1951 after Franklin D. Roosevelt won four terms, states plainly: "No person shall be elected to the office of the President more than twice."

Amending the Constitution requires a two-thirds majority vote in both the House and Senate, followed by ratification by three-fourths of state legislatures — a process that typically takes years. House Speaker Mike Johnson addressed the issue directly last October, telling reporters he saw no path to changing the Constitution on this matter, according to Reuters.

"It's been a great run. But I think the president knows, and he and I have talked about, the constrictions of the Constitution," Johnson said.

Jokes or Trial Balloons?

Constitutional scholars and political observers have debated whether Trump's remarks represent genuine political ambitions or strategic trolling of his critics. Trump, 80, will be 82 at the end of his current term in January 2029.

The Trump Organization continues to sell "Trump 2028" hats for $50 on its merchandise website. Earlier this year, Trump also joked about getting "out of office in, let's say, eight or nine years from now," and during a July 4 speech marking the United States Semiquincentennial, he quipped about serving a third term, according to reporting compiled by multiple outlets.

Allies like Steve Bannon have been more direct. In an October 2025 interview with The Economist, Bannon said Trump was "going to get a third term" and that a "plan" was being developed, though no details have materialized, according to Poynter.

What's Next

With the 2028 presidential election more than two years away, the question of succession within the Republican Party remains open. Trump has not endorsed a successor. Vice President Vance has avoided questions about a 2028 bid, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last year that Vance would have his support if he ran.

For now, Trump continues to walk a line between constitutional acknowledgment and performative ambiguity — a strategy that keeps him at the center of the 2028 conversation even as the law makes him ineligible to run.
nri_angle: Trump's repeated flirtation with the idea of extending his time in office raises questions about democratic norms that resonate with immigrants who chose the U.S. for its institutional stability.
